Name: Norse Paganism
Description: Pre-Christian polytheistic religion of the Norse people, emphasizing honor, fate, and the cosmic struggle between order and chaos.
CreationMyth: In the beginning was Ginnungagap, the void between fire (Muspelheim) and ice (Niflheim). When fire and ice met, the giant Ymir was born from the melting ice. The first god, Búri, emerged from ice licked by the cow Auðumbla. Búri's grandsons—Odin, Vili, and Vé—slew Ymir and created the world from his body: his flesh became earth, his blood the seas, his bones the mountains, his hair the trees, and his skull the sky. From two tree trunks they created the first humans, Ask and Embla, giving them breath, consciousness, and form. The gods built Asgard in the sky, connected to Midgard (the human world) by the rainbow bridge Bifröst.
CorePrinciples: Honor and reputation (frith) paramount
Fate (wyrd) is inescapable, even for gods
Courage in face of inevitable doom (Ragnarök)
Reciprocity and gift-giving build relationships
Strength and martial prowess valued
Connection to ancestors and land
Nine worlds connected by Yggdrasil, the World Tree
NotableFigures: Odin (All-Father, god of wisdom and war)

Name: Ancient Greek Religion
Description: Polytheistic religion of ancient Greece centered on the Olympian gods, emphasizing ritual, sacrifice, and human excellence.
CreationMyth: In the beginning was Chaos, the void. From Chaos emerged Gaia (Earth), Tartarus (the underworld), and Eros (love). Gaia gave birth to Ouranos (Sky), and together they produced the Titans. The Titan Kronos overthrew Ouranos, then swallowed his own children to prevent being overthrown. Zeus, hidden by his mother Rhea, escaped and led the Olympian gods in a ten-year war (Titanomachy) against the Titans. Zeus and his siblings—Poseidon, Hades, Hera, Demeter, and Hestia—defeated the Titans and established rule from Mount Olympus. Prometheus shaped humans from clay, and Athena breathed life into them. Zeus punished Prometheus for giving fire to humans by chaining him to a rock.
CorePrinciples: Hubris (excessive pride) leads to nemesis (downfall)
Honor the gods through ritual and sacrifice
Arete: excellence and virtue in all endeavors
Fate (moira) governs all, even gods
Hospitality (xenia) is sacred
Know thyself (Delphic maxim)
Nothing in excess (Delphic maxim)

Name: Ancient Egyptian Religion
Description: Complex polytheistic religion emphasizing the afterlife, cosmic order (ma'at), and the divine pharaoh.
Sources: Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day)
CreationMyth: In the beginning was Nun, the primordial waters of chaos. From Nun emerged the benben, the primordial mound, upon which the creator god Atum appeared. Atum was alone and complete in himself. Through his own power, he created Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture), who in turn gave birth to Geb (earth) and Nut (sky). From Geb and Nut came Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys. Atum/Ra became the sun god, traveling across the sky by day in his solar barque and through the underworld (Duat) by night, battling the chaos serpent Apophis to ensure the sun would rise again. Humans were created from the tears of Ra.
CorePrinciples: Ma'at: cosmic order, truth, justice, and balance
Afterlife more important than earthly life
Pharaoh is divine intermediary between gods and humans
Heart weighed against feather of Ma'at in judgment
Preservation of body (mummification) for afterlife
Ka (life force), ba (personality), akh (spirit) survive death
Cyclical time: death and rebirth like daily sun

Name: Mesopotamian Religion (Sumerian/Babylonian)
Description: Polytheistic religion of ancient Mesopotamia emphasizing service to capricious gods and acceptance of human limitations.
CreationMyth: In the beginning, only Apsu (fresh water) and Tiamat (salt water) existed, their waters mingling. From their union came the first gods, whose noise disturbed Apsu. He planned to destroy them, but the god Ea killed Apsu first. Tiamat, enraged, created monsters and chose Kingu as her champion. The young god Marduk agreed to fight Tiamat if the other gods made him supreme king. He defeated Tiamat, split her body in half to create heaven and earth, and used Kingu's blood to create humans. Humans were created as servants to the gods, to feed them through sacrifice and relieve them of labor. The gods built the city of Babylon and the great ziggurat Etemenanki as Marduk's dwelling place.
CorePrinciples: Humans created to serve the gods
Gods are powerful but capricious and petty
Fate is controlled by divine council, not individual will
Death is final; underworld is gloomy shadow existence
Cities and temples are centers of divine presence
Kings rule by divine mandate
Accept human mortality and limitations

Name: Aztec Religion
Description: Complex polytheistic religion emphasizing cosmic cycles, human sacrifice to maintain universal order, and the dual nature of existence.
Sources: Historia de las Indias de Nueva España (Diego Durán)
CreationMyth: The world has been created and destroyed four times before the current era (the Fifth Sun). In the beginning, the dual god Ometeotl divided into male and female aspects, creating the four Tezcatlipocas and Quetzalcoatl. These gods created the earth from the body of the earth monster Cipactli. Four previous worlds (suns) were each destroyed by jaguars, wind, fire, and flood. The current Fifth Sun was created at Teotihuacan when the gods sacrificed themselves, and the humble god Nanahuatzin threw himself into a fire to become the sun. But the sun wouldn't move until the other gods sacrificed their blood. Quetzalcoatl descended to the underworld (Mictlan) and retrieved the bones of previous humans, sprinkling them with his own blood to create humanity. Humans must maintain the sun through blood sacrifice.
CorePrinciples: Blood sacrifice necessary to maintain cosmic order
Duality: life/death, order/chaos in constant balance
Current world (Fifth Sun) will inevitably end
Humans created to nourish gods with blood
Warfare to capture sacrificial victims (Flower Wars)
Calendrical precision: 260-day ritual and 365-day solar
Warrior's death or childbirth death grants paradise
NotableFigures: Quetzalcoatl (feathered serpent, god of wind and learning)

Name: Yoruba Religion
Description: Traditional religion of the Yoruba people emphasizing a supreme creator, intermediary orishas, and ancestor veneration.
CreationMyth: In the beginning, there was only Olodumare, the supreme creator, and the primordial waters below the sky. Olodumare sent the orisha Obatala down with a chain, a snail shell with sand, and a chicken to create land. But Obatala drank palm wine and fell asleep, so Olodumare sent Oduduwa instead to spread the sand and let the chicken scratch it to create the first land at Ile-Ife, the sacred city. Obatala later molded humans from clay, but when he drank palm wine while working, he created people with disabilities; afterward, he became their protector. Olodumare breathed life into the clay forms. The orishas are divine forces of nature and human experience, intermediaries between Olodumare and humanity. Each person has a destiny (ori) chosen before birth.
CorePrinciples: Olodumare is supreme, distant creator
Orishas as intermediaries: forces of nature and archetypes
Ancestor veneration maintains family lineage
Divination (Ifá) reveals destiny and guidance
Ashe: spiritual power/life force in all things
Each person has ori (destiny/inner head)
Balance between opposing forces

Name: Lakota Spirituality
Description: Sacred traditions of the Lakota people emphasizing harmony with nature, the sacred hoop of life, and the interconnectedness of all beings through the concept of Mitakuye Oyasin (all my relations).
CreationMyth: In the time before time, Inyan (Rock), the first being, was all that existed. Feeling lonely, Inyan created Maka (Earth) from himself, bleeding out his blue blood which became the waters. Han (Darkness) was the first spirit. Wi (Sun) was created to light the world, and Skan (Sky) gave motion and life. The sacred White Buffalo Calf Woman appeared to the Lakota people, teaching them the Seven Sacred Rites and gifting them the sacred pipe (chanunpa). She told them to honor all their relatives—the two-legged, four-legged, winged ones, and all living things. She promised to return in times of need. The sacred hoop represents the cycle of life, with the four directions each holding sacred teachings.
CorePrinciples: Mitakuye Oyasin: All my relations - interconnectedness of all life
Wakan Tanka: The Great Mystery/Great Spirit pervades all
Four sacred directions hold teachings and spiritual guardians
Sacred hoop: circle of life, seasons, generations
Vision quests for spiritual guidance and purpose
Sweat lodge (inipi) for purification and prayer
Pipe ceremony connects earth and sky, humans and spirits
Respect for Earth as mother, provider of all needs
Seven generations principle: consider impact on future descendants
NotableFigures: Sitting Bull (Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man)
Crazy Horse (Oglala Lakota warrior and vision seeker)
Black Elk (Oglala Lakota medicine man and visionary)
Regions: Great Plains (North and South Dakota, Montana, Wyoming)
Sacred sites: Black Hills (He Sapa), Bear Butte, Badlands

Name: Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace
Description: Constitutional and spiritual framework of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, emphasizing peace, democracy, and the balance of power through clan mothers and sachems, considered one of the world's oldest participatory democracies.
CreationMyth: In ancient times, the five nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca) were locked in cycles of violence and blood feuds. The Peacemaker (Deganawida) was born among the Huron with a divine mission to end warfare. With his spokesman Hiawatha, who had lost his family to violence, the Peacemaker traveled among the nations teaching the principles of peace, unity, and the power of good minds. He convinced the violent sorcerer Tadodaho to embrace peace by combing the snakes from his hair. Under the Great Tree of Peace at Onondaga, the Peacemaker buried weapons of war, planted the tree with white roots reaching in four directions, and placed an eagle on top as guardian. The confederacy was established with 50 hereditary sachems chosen by clan mothers, creating a system of checks and balances.
CorePrinciples: Great Law of Peace: constitution governing confederacy relations
Power of Good Mind: rational thought and peace over emotion and war
Consensus decision-making in Grand Council
Clan Mothers select and can remove sachems (chiefs)
Seven generations principle: consider impact of decisions
Tree of Peace: four white roots of peace extend to all nations
Wampum belts record treaties and constitutional provisions
Condolence ceremony heals grief and maintains peace
Women hold power over land, agriculture, and governance
NotableFigures: Jigonsaseh (Mother of Nations, first clan mother)
Tadodaho (transformed from sorcerer to first Onondaga sachem)
Regions: Northeastern North America (New York, Ontario, Quebec)

Name: Māori Cosmology
Description: Spiritual worldview of the Māori people emphasizing whakapapa (genealogy connecting all things), tapu (sacredness), mana (spiritual power/authority), and the balance between Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) and Ranginui (Sky Father).
CreationMyth: In the beginning, Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) were locked in an eternal embrace, their children trapped in darkness between them. The children debated separating their parents. Tāne Mahuta (god of forests) placed his shoulders against his mother and feet against his father, pushing them apart to create light and space. This caused great grief—Ranginui's tears became rain, Papatūānuku's sighs became mist rising from the earth. Tāne created the first woman, Hineahuone, from earth and breathed life into her. Their daughter Hinetītama later became Hine-nui-te-pō, goddess of death, after learning Tāne was her father. Māui, the trickster demigod, fished up the North Island (Te Ika-a-Māui) and attempted to defeat death by crawling through Hine-nui-te-pō, but was crushed, making death permanent for humans.
CorePrinciples: Whakapapa: genealogy connects all beings from gods to humans to nature
Tapu: sacred restrictions protecting spiritual power
Mana: spiritual authority and prestige earned through actions
Kaitiakitanga: guardianship/stewardship of land and resources
Mauri: life force present in all things
Utu: reciprocity, balance, and restoration of harmony
Whanaungatanga: kinship connections and responsibilities
Tino rangatiratanga: self-determination and sovereignty
Whenua: land as foundation of identity (placenta also means land)
NotableFigures: Ranginui and Papatūānuku (Sky Father and Earth Mother)
Tāne Mahuta (god of forests and birds)
Te Whiti o Rongomai (prophet of passive resistance, 19th century)

Name: Andean/Incan Religion
Description: Cosmovision of the Inca Empire and broader Andean peoples emphasizing reciprocity with nature, ancestor veneration, and the sacred relationship between humans, earth (Pachamama), and the cosmos.
Sources: Oral traditions (preserved through quipu knot records)
Archaeological evidence from temples and sacred sites
CreationMyth: In the time of darkness before the current age, the creator god Viracocha emerged from Lake Titicaca and created the sun, moon, and stars. He molded humans from stone at Tiwanaku, breathing life into them. Displeased with the first creation, he sent a great flood to destroy them, then created a second humanity. Viracocha traveled teaching arts and agriculture, and two brothers helped spread his teachings. He walked across the waters of the Pacific, promising to return. The sun god Inti sent his children, Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, from Lake Titicaca with a golden staff to find the place where it would sink into the earth. At Cusco, the staff sank, and there they founded the Inca Empire. Inca rulers claimed descent from Inti, making them divine intermediaries.
CorePrinciples: Ayni: reciprocity and mutual obligation between humans and nature
Pachamama: Earth Mother who provides and must be honored with offerings
Inti: Sun god as source of life and ancestor of Inca royalty
Huacas: sacred places, objects, and beings imbued with spiritual power
Ancestor veneration: mummified rulers consulted for guidance
Mit'a: reciprocal labor obligation to community and empire
Three realms: Hanan Pacha (upper/celestial), Kay Pacha (middle/earthly), Ukhu Pacha (inner/underworld)
Capacocha: ritual sacrifice of children at sacred mountains
Quipu: knotted strings recording information and prayers
NotableFigures: Pachacuti (Inca emperor who expanded empire, 15th century)
Regions: Andean highlands (Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile, Argentina)
Sacred sites: Machu Picchu, Cusco, Lake Titicaca, Sacsayhuamán

Name: Sami Shamanism
Description: Animistic spiritual tradition of the Sami people emphasizing shamanic journeying (noaidi practices), reverence for nature spirits, and the sacred drum as gateway to other realms.
Sources: Written accounts by missionaries and ethnographers
CreationMyth: In the beginning, Radien-attje (the Creator) and Maderakka (Earth Mother) created the world. Maderakka has three daughters who assist in human life: Sarakka guides childbirth, Juksakka protects children, and Uksakka guards the doorway. The world has three realms: the upper world (where gods dwell), middle world (where humans and nature spirits live), and underworld (where Jabmeaimo, land of the dead, is located). The cosmic pillar connects these realms. Bieggolmai (Wind Man) was sent by Radien to help early humans survive the harsh north. The noaidi (shaman) can journey between these realms using the runebomme (sacred drum) and enter ecstatic trance to communicate with spirits, heal sickness, and predict the future.
CorePrinciples: Animism: all natural phenomena have spirits/souls
Noaidi: shaman travels between realms for healing and guidance
Runebomme: sacred drum for divination and spirit communication
Sieidi: sacred stones and sites with spiritual power
Reindeer herding as sacred partnership with animals
Joik/yoik: improvised song-poems honoring persons, places, or animals
Respect for siida: traditional community and land use
Offering sites at significant landscape features
Three souls: free soul (travels in dreams), body soul, breath soul
NotableFigures: Historical noaidi (shamans) - names lost to forced conversion
Áillohaš (Johan Turi, early 20th c. author preserving traditions)
Regions: Sápmi (traditional Sami lands spanning Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia)
Arctic and subarctic regions of Northern Scandinavia and Kola Peninsula
